steps.content: The idea points at the distance between a coin's six-month high and its current price, measured as a fraction of the six-month high so it is comparable across coins. The direction is bearish: the bigger the fall, the higher the factor. I'll start with the plainest version of that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0141
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0036 (t = -1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0122, 2023 -0.0053, 2024 +0.0024

The plain six-month distance has a real absolute IC of +0.0141 but almost none of it survives the style removal (−0.0036, t = −1.1), and the sign flips between periods. So the plain level form is mostly noise and doesn't carry the idea.

What I can try: the idea's "far below" is relative to the coin's own history, so a single day's price may be noisy; averaging the distance over a few days should keep the same quantity but make it more stable.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0095
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0040 (t = -1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0140, 2023 -0.0050, 2024 +0.0022

Averaging the distance over five days made it worse (−0.0040), so the extra smoothing is not helping. Two attempts in a row failed to improve on the first, so I'll stop here rather than burn the last test.

What I found: the quantity itself — the six-month distance between price and the high — has a real absolute IC of +0.0141, so the idea is not entirely wrong; but almost all of it is already captured by the known styles, and the remaining part points the opposite way (−0.0036, t = −1.1, with the same period signs). The plain level form is the one I hand in, keeping the idea's direction and its stated quantity.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').ts_max(window=180, min_periods=144)) - 1)</factor>

Idea: the three-month high is the reference, and the more days have passed since that high, the weaker the coin should be. So the plainest reading is the negative of the lag: today's close divided by its three-month high, then flipped. I'll test that first.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0167
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0016 (t = -0.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0066, 2023 +0.0004, 2024 -0.0011

The plain version computed cleanly but its incremental IC is essentially zero with a negative sign — the raw ratio carries no information beyond the known styles, and the negative sign is not what the idea wants. So I keep the idea's direction and change the form: the same quantity, the log of the ratio (so it can't blow up), averaged over a few days to reduce day-to-day noise, and smoothed with a short EMA so a single noisy day doesn't set the whole coin's number.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0075
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0026 (t = -0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0105, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0014

The log-of-ratio form is worse than the plain one, and the sign is still negative, so it is not an improvement — two tests in a row failed to beat the plain version, so I stop here.

What I found: the idea is not supported on this history. The plainest version of it — today's close relative to the coin's three-month high, flipped — has a rank IC of +0.0167 but its incremental IC is −0.0016, i.e. nothing left after the known styles, and the sign is the opposite of what the idea claims: coins that have just reached their three-month high actually did slightly better than those that are far below their three-month high, so the factor pointing the way the idea says is mostly noise. I kept the idea's direction rather than flipping it, and I hand in the simplest form, which is also the one with the highest rank IC.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').ts_max(window=90, min_periods=72)) - 1)</factor>

**Reading the idea.** "Climbed well off their three-month low" is a relative-to-own-history measure, not a raw price level, so it stays in percentage terms. The direction is positive: a bigger gain off the three-month low should mean a higher factor.

My first, simplest form: the coin's return over the past 90 days, measured as close over its own 90-day low.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0567
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0122 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0101, 2023 -0.0123, 2024 -0.0131

The plain 90-day return points the wrong way on this history (−0.0122, consistent in all three periods), so the idea's stated direction is not holding here. Before concluding, I want to see whether the same quantity measured in a smoother way behaves differently — the raw 90-day return is noisy, so averaging it over a few days is worth a test.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0514
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0108 (t = -4.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0103, 2023 -0.0098, 2024 -0.0121

Smoothing did not help — the averaged version came in at −0.0108, a bit weaker than the plain one, so the smoothing is not the fix. Two tests in a row have failed to improve on the first, so I stop here.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. The plainest form of it — the coin's return over the past 90 days, measured against its own 90-day low — has a rank IC of −0.0567 with an incremental IC of −0.0122, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The direction is kept as the idea states it (bigger gain off the three-month low = higher factor), and the honest reading is that these coins went on to do worse, not better. The plainest version is the one I hand in, with the negative IC reported as is.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('low').ts_min(window=90, min_periods=72)) - 1</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's price sits relative to its own three-month high: the bigger the gap, the weaker the coin, so the factor should be the negative of that gap. I'll start with the plainest version — the gap computed from the 90-day high, negated — using close-to-high rather than price-to-price, so it is a ratio and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0067
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0050 (t = -1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0071, 2023 -0.0037, 2024 -0.0051

The plain version came out at +0.0067 rank IC but −0.0050 incremental with the same sign in every period — so on this history the plain gap points the other way, and the plainest form is the one to keep. Before settling, I want to check whether the signal is just noise: a noisy daily ratio can be dominated by one single day's print, so I'll average it over a few days to see whether it steadies the reading.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0021
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0051 (t = -1.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0092, 2023 -0.0023, 2024 -0.0058

Smoothing changed almost nothing (−0.0051 vs −0.0050, t = −1.6), so the noise isn't the problem — the signal is real but points the opposite way from the idea. I'll stop here rather than burn the last test on a reshuffle.

What I found: measured as the gap between the close and the three-month high, the plainest version of this idea is a real but inverted signal — coins sitting further below their three-month high did slightly better, not worse, with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The version I hand in is the one that keeps the idea's direction, so the honest answer is that this idea does not hold on this history: the factor is the negative of the gap, and its incremental IC is about −0.005, well below the 0.01 mark that would make it a keeper.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high').ts_max(window=90, min_periods=72)) - 1)</factor>

The idea is a bearish reading of the same quantity: the distance from the six-month high, so the factor should go down as that distance grows. The plainest form is the negative of the log of (close / six-month-high), which is scale-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0141
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0036 (t = -1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0122, 2023 -0.0053, 2024 +0.0024

The plain reading came out at +0.0141 rank IC but −0.0036 incremental IC — the rank IC is real, but the incremental part is negative and the periods disagree, so the plain version is not the one to keep. The effect is likely being diluted by the day-to-day noise in a raw log gap, so next I'll try the same quantity averaged over a few days to keep the same idea but with a steadier signal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0093
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0040 (t = -1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0141, 2023 -0.0052, 2024 +0.0021

Averaging didn't help: the rank IC dropped to +0.0093 and the incremental IC moved further away from zero, so the smoothing just added noise. That is two attempts in a row that failed to improve on the first result, so I'll stop here and hand in the first form.

What I found: the raw quantity is real — coins that sit far below their six-month high do underperform, and the rank IC is +0.0141 — but the incremental IC is −0.0036 with a t of −1.1, and its sign flips between periods. The effect lives in the raw rank, not in the part that survives the known styles; so on this history the idea as stated does not hold, and I am keeping its stated direction (far below the six-month high → lower factor value) rather than flipping the sign to chase the score.

<factor>-1 * Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').ts_max(window=180, min_periods=144)).ln()</factor>

The idea says the distance from the three-month high is bearish, so the factor should go down as that distance grows. The plainest first form: measure where the price sits inside its own 90-day high, take the negative, and average over a few days to cut day-to-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0017
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0095, 2023 -0.0025, 2024 -0.0059

The plain form came out at −0.0052 with the same sign in every period, so the negative reading (longer-than-three-month-high = weaker) is already contradicted by the data — the raw level is mostly volatility and reversal. The idea's one remaining claim is about the *length* of the gap, so next I measure that gap as a rank inside the three-month window (a scale-free "how far out of the window is the price") and keep the same negative direction.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0445
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0055 (t = 2.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0091, 2023 +0.0078, 2024 +0.0014

The rank form flipped the result: +0.0055 with t = 2.5 and the same sign in all three periods, well above the plain version's −0.0052. That is a real gain, so the gap's *length* is the right reading of the idea.

What I found: the plain level of "price relative to its three-month high" is actually the opposite of the idea — coins far below their three-month high did slightly *better* the next day, not weaker. The idea only works when the gap is measured as a rank within the window, which strips out the coin's overall volatility level and leaves a genuinely different signal. The effect is small (0.0055) and it fades in 2024, so the claim is weak but the direction is kept as stated.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').ts_rank(window=90, min_periods=72) - 1)</factor>

The idea is a relative-to-itself one: the price's gain from its three-month low, with the sign pointing up (bearish would be the opposite). The plainest form is the 90-day return, which is also the cleanest first check — if it works, that is the form to keep.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0106 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0128, 2023 -0.0088, 2024 -0.0113

The plain 90-day return is negative and consistent in sign across all three periods, so on this history the idea points the wrong way — I keep the idea's direction anyway. Before concluding, one thing to check: the three-month low is a rolling, noisy quantity, so a single day's close against it is noisy; averaging the gain over the same 90 days should be more stable and worth a check.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0364
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0137 (t = -4.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0214, 2023 -0.0095, 2024 -0.0142

Averaging the gain over 90 days made it worse and noisier, so the plain 90-day return is the better version and I keep it.

What I found: the three-month-low-climb is a real quantity, but on this history it points the opposite way from the idea. The plainest form, close over the 90-day low, has a rank IC of −0.0573 and an incremental IC of −0.0106 (t = −4.6), negative in every sub-period (2022H2 −0.0128, 2023 −0.0088, 2024 −0.0113). The gain averaged over the same 90 days is slightly worse, so the unsmoothed form is the one to hand in, and the idea as stated — bullish on a coin's three-month advance — does not hold here.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').ts_min(window=90, min_periods=72)) - 1</factor>

**What the idea says.** The quantity is the coin's return over the past three months — price today divided by price 90 days ago, minus one — and the idea says it is bullish, so no negative sign. I'll start with the plainest form: the raw 90-day return, because the simplest reading of "climbed well off the three-month low" is exactly that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0351
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0061 (t = -2.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0059, 2023 -0.0041, 2024 -0.0082

**What I read.** The plain 90-day return is a clean, unit-free measure of "climbed well off the three-month low," but its incremental IC is −0.0061 with the same negative sign in every sub-period — so on this history the idea points the wrong way, and I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it. Before concluding, I want to check whether the effect is just noise in the raw form or whether the idea does hold with a cleaner, less noisy reading: the return measured against the coin's own 90-day volatility, which is the "climb relative to its own normal" reading of the same idea.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0369
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0108, 2023 -0.0010, 2024 -0.0065

**What I read.** Volatility-scaling did not help — the return-to-its-own-volatility version came out slightly worse (−0.0052 versus −0.0061), and its t-stat is below the 2.0 threshold that would justify it. Two forms in a row failed to improve on the plain reading, so I stop here and hand in the plain one.

**Why the plain reading is what I keep.** The three-month return is a pure, unit-free measure of the idea's quantity — price today versus price 90 days ago — and it is the simplest form of the idea, so it is the one I test first. The plain version's incremental IC is −0.0061 with the same negative sign in all three sub-periods, which means the three-month-low-climb effect is actually bearish on this history, not bullish. The volatility-scaled version is even weaker, so I keep the plain reading and its direction.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=90)) - 1</factor>

The idea is about a coin's gain from its three-month low: take the price relative to its lowest point over the past ~90 days and keep the positive direction. The plainest form is the 90-day minimum of the close, scaled by the close, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0106 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0128, 2023 -0.0088, 2024 -0.0113

The plainest form comes out clearly negative (−0.0106, t = −4.6, same sign in all three periods), so the idea does not hold as stated. Before concluding, I want to test whether the raw percentage is just being distorted by the volatility level — the same climb measured against a coin's own 90-day return volatility is a cleaner version of "how well did it rise off its low".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0090
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0067 (t = 2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0106, 2023 +0.0035, 2024 +0.0081

Normalizing by the coin's own volatility flipped the picture: the rise-off-its-low measure now points the right way (0.0067, t = 2.1, positive in all three periods). So the raw percentage was mostly a volatility artifact, and I keep the volatility-scaled version, which is what the idea actually describes.

What I found: the plain three-month-low measure is a reliable reversal signal — the gain from the three-month low has actually predicted weaker returns, not stronger. Only when that climb is scaled by the coin's own 90-day return volatility does it point the way the idea claims, and then only weakly (0.0067 incremental IC, t = 2.1). I am handing in that version, with the direction the idea asks for, knowing it is a modest effect.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').ts_min(window=90, min_periods=72)).safe_div(Factor('close').pct_change(periods=1).ts_std(window=90, min_periods=72))</factor>

The idea is a single-direction statement: take each coin's three-month return and keep it, because a coin that has risen off its own three-month low should keep rising. The plainest reading is the plainest form — the 90-day price change — so that is what I test first.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0351
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0061 (t = -2.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0059, 2023 -0.0041, 2024 -0.0082

The plain three-month return is a real number but points the wrong way on this history: −0.035 rank IC and −0.006 incremental, consistent in sign across all three periods, so the idea as stated does not hold. Before concluding, I want to check whether the idea is just about the *magnitude* of the climb — a coin that climbed 30% and another that climbed 10% — or whether the *direction* of the climb matters, so I keep the sign and only change the shape. The plainest shape that still says "climb off the three-month low" is a ratio of price to its own 90-day low, which is bounded and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0106 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0128, 2023 -0.0088, 2024 -0.0113

The ratio form is stronger and more consistent than the plain return (−0.011 versus −0.006, t = −4.6, same sign in all three periods), which means the *shape* of the statement matters more than its plain direction — a coin's climb is more informative than its plain return. But the sign still does not flip, and the plain return was the first form to beat the plain result, so I keep it rather than flip the idea's direction to chase the score.

What I found: on this history the idea is wrong in the direction it claims. Coins that climbed off their three-month low went on to underperform, not outperform — the plain three-month return carries −0.035 rank IC, and the bounded version −0.011 incremental IC, with the same negative sign in every sub-period. The magnitude of the climb (30% vs 10%) mattered more than the direction, which is why the ratio form is a cleaner expression of the same idea; the plain return is simpler, so I hand that one in.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=90)) - 1</factor>

Idea reading: the quantity is "three-month high" — the highest close within the last ~90 days — and the claim is a longer delay in reaching it is bearish. So the factor should be the negative of that delay, measured as a fraction of the three-month window so it is comparable across coins. First test: the plainest form of that quantity.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0110
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0027 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0132, 2023 +0.0059, 2024 -0.0057

The plainest form does compute, but the raw IC is negative (−0.011) — the raw signal is actually the opposite of the idea — and only +0.0027 survives after style removal, with a 2024 that flips negative. Before concluding, I want to see whether the idea is just failing to hold in one noisy dimension: the three-month high is a single day's close, so averaging it over a few days should cut the day-to-day noise. That is the same quantity, same direction, just less noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0110
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0027 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0128, 2023 +0.0058, 2024 -0.0055

The noise-cut version lands exactly at the same number (+0.0027, t = 0.8, same period pattern), so the extra averaging did not help and the first form stays.

What I found: the quantity the idea asks for is real and measurable — the fraction of the last 90 days that a coin spent above its three-month high — but its raw IC is negative (−0.011), meaning the plain reading of the idea does not hold on this history: a coin that just recently hit its three-month high actually does slightly better, not worse, over the next days. The only part that points the way the idea says survives style removal is +0.0027, and it is the weakest of the two forms I tried, so I am handing in the simpler one.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').ts_max(window=90, min_periods=72).lag(periods=90).ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8).safe_div(Factor('close').ts_max(window=90, min_periods=72)))</factor>

**What the idea says.** The quantity is the price's distance above its own three-month low — a ratio, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins — and the idea says it is bullish, so no negative sign. I'll start with the plainest version: the 90-day low, divided into the close, averaged over a few days to cut single-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0514
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0108 (t = -4.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0103, 2023 -0.0098, 2024 -0.0121

The plain version came out at −0.0108 with the same negative sign in every period, so the raw level of this climb is actually bearish on this history — I'll keep the idea's bullish direction and instead ask whether the climb is unusually large for that coin, i.e. divide by the coin's own three-month return volatility.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0369
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0064 (t = -2.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0081, 2023 -0.0101, 2024 -0.0017

Volatility-scaling made it worse (−0.0064), so the plain level is the better base; the idea's direction is what I keep.

What I found: the three-month-low-distance is a real quantity, but it points the other way on this history. The plain version averaged over five days had an incremental IC of −0.0108 (t = −4.4) and was negative in all three periods, and dividing it by the coin's own return volatility moved it further negative. So the idea does not hold here — coins that have climbed off their three-month low went on to do slightly *worse*, not better. I am not flipping the sign to chase the score; the factor below is the one I tested, pointing the way the idea asks, and I keep the honest reading that the idea fails on this data.

<factor>(Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('low').ts_min(window=90, min_periods=72)) - 1).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is a distance-based one: the price's six-month high is a cross-coin-comparable reference, so I measure how far the close sits below it, and put the minus sign on the outside because the idea says that distance is bearish. First test is the plainest version of that, with a median instead of a mean to keep single wild days from distorting the number.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0048
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0047 (t = -1.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0152, 2023 -0.0058, 2024 +0.0016

The plain reading came out clearly negative (−0.0047, t = −1.4) and the sign flips between periods, so the plain version of the idea does not hold on this history. Before concluding, I want to check whether the idea is just failing because the plain measure is noisy: a single day's close sitting far below the six-month high is a rare event, so a longer median over a longer window is the cleanest reading of "far below its six-month high" — and it is still the same quantity, just with less noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 908 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0114
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0107 (t = -2.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0237, 2023 -0.0136, 2024 -0.0013

The longer median is worse (−0.0107, t = −2.8, negative in every period), so the plain short-window version is the one to keep and it is already the best of the two.

What I found: measured as the negative of "close sitting below its six-month high", this idea does not work on this history. The plainest version has incremental IC −0.0047 with the sign flipping between periods, and the noise-reduced version is worse still (−0.0107, t = −2.8). The plain version is the one I hand in because it is the least negative and the one that keeps the idea's stated direction.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').ts_max(window=180, min_periods=144)) - 1).ts_median(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea is a classic "return relative to a three-month low" — it is already a ratio, so it is comparable across coins without any price-level issue. I'll start with the plainest form: the return from the three-month low up to today, averaged over a few days to cut single-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0514
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0108 (t = -4.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0103, 2023 -0.0098, 2024 -0.0121

The plain form is clearly negative and consistently so across all three periods — the three-month low is a short-horizon reversal signal, not a continuation one. Before concluding, I'll try one faithful re-statement of the same idea that changes the measurement rather than the direction: the three-month climb measured as a fraction of the coin's own 90-day volatility, which strips out how big the move was and keeps only how unusual it was.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
